units.title: The Five Mother Sauces
units.summary: Béchamel, velouté, espagnole, tomato and hollandaise – the foundation of classical sauce making.
units.objective: Identify the five classical mother sauces, their liquids, thickening methods and a common derivative of each.
units.cip: CIP 12.0508 – Sauce production (alignment to be confirmed by instructor)
miniLesson: Classical French cuisine organizes sauces into families. Each family begins with a mother (or leading) sauce. Adding ingredients to a mother sauce creates a derivative, or small, sauce.

Three of the five are built on a liquid plus a roux: béchamel (milk), velouté (white stock) and espagnole (brown stock). Tomato sauce is thickened by the tomato itself, and hollandaise is an emulsion of egg yolks and butter.
Why it matters: when you understand the family, you can troubleshoot lumps, breaking, or thin texture, and create new sauces with confidence.

definitions.text: A cooked mixture of equal weights of fat and flour used to thicken liquids.
A mixture of two liquids that normally do not combine, held together by an emulsifier such as egg yolk.
A sauce made by adding ingredients to a mother sauce.
Thick enough to coat the back of a spoon.

table.caption: The five mother sauces at a glance

knowledgeCheck.stem: Which mother sauce is made from milk thickened with a white roux?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Béchamel is milk plus white roux. Velouté uses a white stock.

options.text: An emulsion of egg yolks and butter

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Hollandaise is an emulsion. Warm egg yolks hold clarified butter in suspension.

knowledgeCheck.stem: Mornay sauce is a derivative of which mother sauce?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Mornay is béchamel finished with cheese.

knowledgeCheck.stem: Which stock is the base of espagnole?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Espagnole is brown stock thickened with a brown roux, with browned mirepoix and tomato product.

knowledgeCheck.stem: Your béchamel has lumps. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Cold roux added to cold milk without whisking

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Lumps form when the liquid and roux are combined without enough agitation, or when the temperature relationship is wrong. Add liquid gradually while whisking.

exitTicket.prompt: Choose one mother sauce. Explain in two sentences how it is thickened and name one dish where you would use a derivative.

units.reflection: Which sauce was hardest to remember, and what will you do tomorrow to practice it?

units.title: Stocks and Soups
units.summary: Stock types, production methods, quality standards, and the major soup categories.
units.objective: Distinguish the main stock types and soup categories, and describe how to produce a clear, flavorful stock.
units.cip: CIP 12.0508 – Stocks, soups and sauces (alignment to be confirmed by instructor)
miniLesson: A stock is a flavorful liquid made by gently simmering bones, mirepoix and aromatics in water. It is the foundation of soups and sauces.

Production methods: start with cold water so proteins release slowly, simmer – never boil – and skim impurities. Boiling clouds the stock and emulsifies fat. Cool stock quickly and safely before storage.

Quality standards: a good stock is clear, has a clean flavor of its main ingredient, and carries body from gelatin. Soups fall into two broad groups: clear soups (broths, consommé) and thick soups (cream, purée, bisque, chowder).

definitions.text: A flavor base of onion, carrot and celery (classically 2:1:1 by weight).
Herbs and spices tied in cheesecloth for easy removal.
A clarified, crystal-clear soup made with a raft of egg whites and lean meat.
A thick soup traditionally made from shellfish.

table.caption: Common stocks
rows: Chicken, veal or beef bones, unroasted
Roast bones and mirepoix, add tomato

knowledgeCheck.stem: Why should a stock be simmered and not boiled?

options.text: Boiling clouds the stock and emulsifies fat

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Vigorous boiling breaks up particles and emulsifies fat into the liquid, giving a cloudy, greasy stock.
Roasting bones adds color and a deeper flavor to brown stock.
Consommé is a clarified, clear soup. Bisque, chowder and cream soups are thick soups.

options.text: 1 part onion, 1 part carrot, 2 parts celery
2 parts onion, 1 part carrot, 1 part celery
2 parts carrot, 1 part onion, 1 part celery

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Classic mirepoix is 2 parts onion to 1 part carrot to 1 part celery by weight.

knowledgeCheck.stem: Why start a stock with cold water?

options.text: It allows proteins and flavor to be released slowly so impurities can be skimmed
It prevents the bones from cooking

knowledgeCheck.explanation: Starting cold extracts flavor gradually and brings impurities to the surface where you can skim them.

exitTicket.prompt: Describe three things you would check to decide whether a stock meets quality standards.

units.reflection: What is one habit you can use in lab to keep a stock clear and safe to store?
